original_question: Extend the model to n users and m orthogonal channels, where on each slot a user may choose any subset of channels on which to transmit and the receiver reports the per-channel transmitter counts. Is it optimal to run the single-channel capture policy separately and independently on each channel, or can coupling a user's transmission decisions across channels produce strictly better expected time to the first success? More generally, for which combinations of user count and channel count is per-channel independence optimal, and when is cross-channel correlation necessary for optimality?
target_in_paper: The draft is targeting the paper’s separate open multi-channel extension of the channel-capture problem: the author’s concluding open-problems statement flags a “Multi-channel case,” and the accompanying slide deck for arXiv:2110.09638 adds that the arXiv version explores the multi-channel 2-user and 3-user cases. This is a different target from the paper’s main single-channel conjecture/proof thread.
correct_elements: Your draft correctly captures the core thematic issue of the paper’s multi-channel extension: decentralized slotted multiple access over orthogonal channels; exact feedback on how many users transmitted; the objective of minimizing expected time to the first success/capture; and the key structural question of whether channelwise-independent randomization is optimal or whether a user must correlate its simultaneous channel choices across channels.
missing_details: The paper’s base symmetry assumptions need to be carried over explicitly: slotted time; all users know the total user count (and, in the extension, the channel count); users are unlabeled/indistinguishable; and every user independently runs the same randomized algorithm.
The objective should be stated precisely as minimizing the expected time until the first success (equivalently, first capture event), not a throughput, regret, or fairness criterion.
The feedback model should be specified as common end-of-slot feedback giving the exact transmitter-count vector across channels, mirroring the single-channel feedback F[t] = number of transmitters.

The notion of “success” in the multi-channel model must be defined explicitly: e.g. the first slot on which some channel has exactly one transmitter, and the process stops at that first singleton event.
The information structure should be stated: each user’s decision at a slot may depend on the common feedback history and its own private transmission history.
If users may transmit on multiple channels in a slot, the admissible action set should be stated explicitly as choosing any subset of the m orthogonal channels.
The independence-vs-correlation comparison should be defined formally: product-form channel decisions for a user versus allowing arbitrary within-user cross-channel correlation on a slot.

Your draft broadens substantially beyond the paper-faithful target by asking for arbitrary n and m and a full characterization of all (user count, channel count) pairs; the recoverable official formulation only flags the multi-channel case and, in the author’s summary slides for this arXiv paper, specifically says the arXiv version explores the 2-user and 3-user multi-channel cases.
Algebraic items such as ambient ring/field, polynomial degree, homogeneity, nilpotency, and phrases like “for all sufficiently large m” are not part of this paper and are inapplicable here.
refined_question: Under the paper’s decentralized channel-capture model—slotted time; a known number of unlabeled/indistinguishable users; every user independently running the same randomized algorithm; and common end-of-slot feedback that reports, for each orthogonal channel, the exact number of transmitters—what is the optimal policy in the multi-channel cases treated in the arXiv version (notably the 2-user and 3-user cases) for minimizing the expected time until the first singleton transmission on any channel? In particular, if on each slot a user may transmit on any subset of the m channels, is it optimal to choose channels independently channel-by-channel by applying the single-channel capture rule separately on each channel, or can a user strictly reduce the expected first-success time by correlating its simultaneous channel choices across channels?
justification: The recoverable official evidence shows that your draft is not aiming at the paper’s main single-channel conjecture/proposition/theorem thread, but at a later open problem: the paper’s setup is the expected-time-to-first-success capture problem for indistinguishable users under exact count feedback, while the conclusion/open-problems summary explicitly lists a “Multi-channel case,” and the author’s slide deck for the same arXiv work says that the arXiv version explores the multi-channel 2-user and 3-user cases. Your draft gets the right conceptual issue—independence across channels versus cross-channel correlation—but it goes beyond the paper by asking for a full all-(n,m) classification. A paper-faithful rewrite should therefore keep the exact decentralized information structure and capture objective from the single-channel model, while narrowing the multi-channel question to the cases the arXiv version actually indicates it studies.
